To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

infrasound (sound frequency <20 Hz) near the hearing threshold induces changes of neural activity in several brain regions, which are known to play a role in auditory processing, emotional control and autonomic regulation.

the infrasound near-threshold (compared to the no-tone condition) is associated with a stronger activation of right amygdala, right superior temporal gyrust and right superior frontal gyrust, and a weaker activation of the anterior cingulate gyrust.

infrasound, when administered close to or at the individual hearing threshold, may induce changes of functional connectivity in several brain regions, including auditory, emotional and autonomic processing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the investigation of brain function in response to infrasonic stimulation near and above the individual hearing level.
the effects of infrasound (i.e. sounds with a frequency of 0–20 Hz) on the human body.
the investigation of infrasound (sound frequency <20 Hz) as a potential environmental factor in the pathogenesis of chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
infrasound, even when applied below the hearing threshold, can affect the brain’s activity.
infrasound may exert a pathogenic effect on the organism, however further (especially longitudinal studies are required in this regard.
infrasound is not only a physical phenomenon but that it also has a biological and even a psychological impact on the human organism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
infrasound may be a potential environmental risk factor that could contribute to the development of stress-related disorders.
infrasound can be considered as a potential environmental factor that may contribute to the development of chronic stress and/or chronic fatigue syndrome.
infrasound may be regarded as a potential risk factor for human health.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain’s response to IS near the hearing threshold involves several key regions of the limbic system, including amygdala and anterior cingulate, and that these regions may be involved in a complex interplay of emotion regulation and autonomic control, which may be relevant for the pathogenicity of infrasound.

even near-threshold IS stimulation can affect neural processing and connectivity in the brain, which may have implications for the health and well-being of exposed individuals, and should be considered in future research and policy decisions.
infrasound, even at very low sound pressure levels, is not a ‘neutral’ stimulus, but may induce significant changes in neural activity, which may have implications for the human organism.
